operator_scope: live camera, DESTRUCTIVE: eight consecutive frames written compressed from a single buffer
notes: The timing half of the run is a clean pass: eight consecutive compressed encodes at a third of the frame budget, spread 17 us. The buffer lifetime is what fails.
This is why the mirror phase mattered. G4a proved a redirected buffer reaches the card; without it, identical frames here could have been read as the redirect not working at all.

explicitly_established.claim: ONE buffer is not enough: all eight frames were written from distinct sources with distinct compressed sizes, yet the frames on the card are byte-identical. The buffer was reused before the card consumed it.
the failure is silent, not torn: every frame decodes, carries twelve tiles and has offsets matching its SOI markers. Checking only that a frame decodes would have called this a success.
the scene was not static: consecutive stock frames from the same clip differ by up to 16 LSB, so identical compressed frames cannot be explained by the subject
the per-frame length IS taken from each frame's own registration; only the content is shared
eight consecutive compressed encodes cost 13,640-13,657 us each, 33% of the 23.976 budget, with zero frames over budget

explicitly_not_established: WHEN the card actually reads the buffer: the content being uniformly the last frame's is consistent with a late per-frame DMA and with a batched write at clip close, and this run cannot tell them apart
how many buffers would be enough; the firmware's own eight-deep source ring is a hint, not a measurement
whether a larger allocation can be obtained from the writer task at all
anything about thermal behaviour: eight frames is a third of a second
the first-frame-derived capacity question, which this run does not touch

corrections.what_happened: All four frames were fetched with a forced --size of 1,302,528. Frame 4 is really 1,301,504 bytes, so that read ran 1,024 bytes past its end and its hash was not a hash of the file.
corrections.conclusion: Both original claims stand and are now separable: the node length IS per-frame, taken from each frame's own registration, and frame 4 is a 1,024-byte-shorter prefix of the same shared payload. Only the buffer contents are shared; the writer's descriptor handling is per-frame and correct.
corrections.note: BUFFER_DESIGN.md cites this as 'the fourth encode's length does not match the file read back' and lists the payload-to-descriptor relation as unknown. That particular discrepancy was my measurement, not the camera's behaviour.
